particulars: The size of a team is not stated, though it is known that the Grand Matches of the period were played with eleven players on each side.
No “fresh men” were allowed to act as substitutes on any account.
As to-day, the umpires could be changed during a match, but only by agreement.
Scoring was by “notches” cut on a stick, and “runs” were so termed until c. 1811, though the word “notch” did not finally disappear from the Laws until 1823.
bold_text: and “runs” were so termed until c. 1811, though the word “notch” did not finally disappear from the Laws until 1823.

particulars: The Ball, weighing between 5 and 6 ounces, was to be marked by the umpires so that it could not be changed during a match.
There was no restriction on the width or length of the Bat.
The Pitch was selected by the side which won the toss; this also determined the choice of innings. (Vide Serial Number 11.)
The Wickets, 22 yards apart, consisted each of two stumps and measured 22 by 6 inches, with one bail 6 inches long.
No limit of length was laid down for the Bowling Crease, and the Popping Crease was 3 feet 10 inches from the wicket.
No special rules existed, and there is no mention of any provision for rolling, cutting or covering the pitch during a match.
The choice of innings as at present depended on the “Toss of a Piece of Money.” The number of innings was not stated but in the Grand Matches it was usual for each side to have two innings.

The intervals allowed after a batsman was dismissed, and between innings were the same as at present. The umpires called “Play” three times after which refusal to play was “at the Peril of giving the Game.”

Note to Serial Numbers 8 and 9: prior to 1700 the form of the wicket is doubtful; Nyren (quoting a MS. lent by William Ward) describes a hole cut between the stumps into which the striker had to pop his bat when running a notch, the wicket-keeper having to place the ball in it — origin of the term “Popping”; Haygarth and Pycroft support this and two oil paintings in the M.C.C. Collection show it; Haygarth's suggestion that it lasted to the late eighteenth century has no substance; Goldwin's 1706 description and the 1727 Richmond Articles show the popping hole had disappeared much earlier; touching the umpire's stick appears to have been the forerunner of the Popping Crease.

No mention is made of how notches were made. The umpires adjudicated on good or bad runs, and this presumably included the case of a short run. If the fielding side obstructed a run, the umpires could order a notch to be scored as a penalty.
bold_text: The umpires adjudicated on good or bad runs, and this presumably included the case of a short run.

particulars: There is no reference to Boundaries.
There is no reference to “Lost ball.”
The “Over” was a four-ball one at the end of which the umpire called “Over.”
The bowler was allowed to change ends once only in any innings.
While the term “Dead ball” is not used, the meaning is implicit in the Laws.

A “No ball” was only called when the bowler's “hinder foot” was in front of the bowling crease. It entailed no penalty, and it would seem that the ball was regarded as dead so that the striker could not score off it.
bold_text: it would seem that the ball was regarded as dead so that the striker could not score off it.

particulars: “Byes” and possibly “Leg Byes” are implied though not explicitly mentioned.
“Wides” were not recognised.
The bail had definitely to fall from the top of the stumps for the wicket to be down—if the bail was already off, then as now, a stump must be struck out of the ground with ball in hand.
An injured batsman could retire, and claim to resume his innings later.
Seven of the nine ways in which to-day a batsman can be “Out” have remained unaltered.

“Silver Billy” Beldham is recorded to have stated that he remembered the introduction of the first “L.B.W.” Law as a cure for the “shabby” methods adopted by the batsmen, but the 1744 Laws in fact long previously allowed the umpires to adjudicate on “standing unfair to strike.”
bold_text: the 1744 Laws in fact long previously allowed the umpires to adjudicate on “standing unfair to strike.”

particulars: In the matter of Obstruction, the striker was only out if he left his running ground to prevent a catch; in their running ground either batsman could obstruct a catch, provided they did not use bat or hand for the purpose.

In general the present-day rules applied, but in addition the umpires were to judge of “all frivolous delays, of all Hurts, whether real or pretended, and are discretionally to allow what Time they think proper before the Game goes on again.”
As to-day, the umpires could only order a batsman out on appeal. Each umpire at his own wicket adjudicated on all appeals.

A committee of the Hambledon Club limited the width of the bat to 4¼ inches in the circumstances already described in Chapter 2. This decision, to be later confirmed by the County representatives, is evidence of the Hambledon prestige at this time—the fact that they settled on a width which has remained unaltered since, does credit to their perception.
bold_text: A committee of the Hambledon Club limited the width of the bat to 4¼ inches in the circumstances already described in Chapter 2.

particulars: The Revision of 1774: carried out by a committee representing Kent, Hampshire, Surrey, Sussex, Middlesex and London — the first occasion on record of any meeting of County representatives. No evidence that the 1755 committee was a standing one, so some changes appearing for the first time may previously have been common practice (known to be so for Serial Number 22).
bold_text: the first occasion on record of any meeting of County representatives. No evidence that the 1755 committee was a standing one, so some changes appearing for the first time may previously have been common practice (known to be so for Serial Number 22).

particulars: Substitutes in the field are no longer definitely prohibited, and it appears probable that they were in fact allowed by consent.
There is no reference to the umpires being changed by mutual consent.
The tolerance for the weight of the ball is reduced to be between 5½ and 5¾ ounces.
The limit of 4¼ inches for the width of the bat is confirmed.

The visiting team has choice of pitch and innings—the pitch to be within 30 yards of a point chosen by the home team. Should the game be played at a “Third Place,” i.e. on a neutral ground, the Bowlers are to toss up for choice of pitch and innings.
The Bowling Crease is defined as being 3 feet long on either side of the wicket.
The interval between innings is increased from 10 to 15 minutes. The umpires are only required to call “Play” once instead of three times before deciding a match against a side refusing to play.

“Short runs” are specially referred to for the first time. (While the Law has remained essentially unaltered, it is of interest to find that a proposal to deduct two runs was considered at the time of the 1835 revision “because such striker, not having run home in the first instance, cannot have started in the second from the proper goal.”)
bold_text: “Short runs” are specially referred to for the first time.

particulars: The umpires are not directed to call “Over.”
The “Hit wicket” Law disappears temporarily.

The first specific “L.B.W.” Law is introduced providing for the striker to be out if he “puts his leg before the wicket with a design to stop the ball, and actually prevents the ball from hitting his wicket by it.” This Law clearly placed a very heavy premium on good umpiring, and it is interesting to note the use of the word “leg” instead of “person,” which appeared later.
The jurisdiction of the umpires for decisions “each at his own wicket” is no longer defined.
The three-stump wicket is introduced, with one bail 6 inches long. (Vide Chapter 2.)
The first reference in an edition of the Laws to the three-stump wicket is found in the Wallis print of this date.
There is a reference to the use of two bails for each wicket in the Maidstone edition of the Laws.
The same edition again contains the “Hit wicket” Law.

The second Maidstone edition includes a new Law dealing with “Obstruction” in identical wording to that later used in the first M.C.C. Code. This reads, “If under pretence of running a Notch, or otherwise, either of the Strikers prevent a Ball from being caught, the Striker of the ball is out.” It might be inferred from this, and from the evidence of Serial Numbers 36 and 37, that a committee carried out some slight revision of the 1774 Code just before the M.C.C. came into being.
bold_text: The second Maidstone edition includes a new Law dealing with “Obstruction” in identical wording to that later used in the first M.C.C. Code. [...] It might be inferred from this, and from the evidence of Serial Numbers 36 and 37, that a committee carried out some slight revision of the 1774 Code just before the M.C.C. came into being.

particulars: The First M.C.C. Code—1788: given in Britcher's Scores (1796) as the Code “revised by the Cricket Club at St. Mary-le-bone, May 30th, 1788.” It is not certain that Britcher may not have incorporated changes approved during the intervening years.
bold_text: It is not certain that Britcher may not have incorporated changes approved during the intervening years.

particulars: The number of stumps is not specified, and this point is not rectified officially until 1838. (Vide Serial Number 83.) It would seem that the three-stump wicket had been so commonly accepted by this year that no special reference to it was thought necessary. Serial Number 36 is not confirmed, and the bail is specified as being 6 inches long.
bold_text: It would seem that the three-stump wicket had been so commonly accepted by this year that no special reference to it was thought necessary.

particulars: For the first time a Law provides for rolling, watering, covering, mowing and beating of the pitch during a match by mutual consent.
It is provided that no run shall be scored if the striker be caught, and that the run in which a batsman is run out shall not be reckoned.
The reintroduction of the “Hit wicket” Law is confirmed in a new form of words.
The application of the “L.B.W.” Law is restricted to a ball which has “pitched in a straight line to the wicket.”
The jurisdiction of the umpires in respect of an appeal for a catch is again introduced.
The provision of substitutes in the field is recognised without restriction as to where they may field.
Permission to change umpires by mutual consent is again granted.
A new ball may be demanded by either side at the start of each innings.

The wicket is increased to measure 24 by 7 inches, with the bail 7 inches long. (The benefits granted to the bowler by Serial Numbers 47 and 48 are particularly interesting as the first evidence of a set policy to maintain an even balance between the bowler and the batsman—vide Chapter 2.)
bold_text: (The benefits granted to the bowler by Serial Numbers 47 and 48 are particularly interesting as the first evidence of a set policy to maintain an even balance between the bowler and the batsman—vide Chapter 2.)

particulars: A new Law provides a penalty of 5 runs if the fieldsman stops a ball with his hat. No doubt the adoption of the top hat as part of the usual attire of the players led to this introduction.
bold_text: No doubt the adoption of the top hat as part of the usual attire of the players led to this introduction.

particulars: The term “Dead ball” is used for the first time in this Law.
The bails are referred to in the plural for the first time in a reliable edition of the Laws.
A “Lost ball” Law is introduced—the striker to score all the runs he may have made, with a minimum allowance of four.
The pitch is to be selected by the umpires within 30 yards of a centre selected by the opposing sides.
annotation: Handwritten (inserted 'in Bold against marginal heading'): The changes listed in Serial Numbers 52 to 56, which all appear in the Laws of 1811, may have been made in 1809, as G. B. Buckley has traced in The Morning Herald of June 1st 1809 a notice which reads, 'A great alteration having taken place in the Laws of Cricket, the new Laws to be had of T. Lord.' (M.S. Extracts, Buckley, G.B.—M.C.C. Library.) This extract reinforces the description of the 1811 Liverpool Edition of the Laws given in Appendix III, and its wording suggests more extensive changes than those contained in Serial Numbers 50 and 51 which are derived from the Wallis broadsheet of May 25th 1809 — this with its engraving would have been in preparation some weeks before the start of the cricket season at which time changes in the Laws would normally be approved. The important alterations contained in Serial Numbers 54, 55 and 56 provide the first evidence of the attack, to develop in later years, against the introduction of round-arm bowling, or 'throwing' as it was then called — vide Chapter 2.

particulars: Tossing is again to decide the choice of innings. It would seem from an examination of unofficial codes that as late as 1828 the old rule by which the visiting side had the choice of pitch and innings continued to be used in the case of Home and Away matches being arranged. The new rule however applied in all other cases, and we can imagine in all the Grand Matches.
The striker is allowed to play at a “No ball,” and to count any resulting runs—he can only be out by being run out.
struck_text: (This change is the first evidence of the attack to develop in the ensuing years against the introduction of round-arm bowling—vide Chapter 2.)

particulars: The term “run” instead of “notch” is seen here for the first time—it became general by 1823.
The ball is to be bowled under-hand and delivered with the hand below the elbow.
struck_text: As in the case of Serial Number 54, we here have evidence of a serious endeavour to obstruct the advent of “throwing-bowling.”

particulars: A Law for “Wides” appears for the first time—the penalty to be one run entered as a “Bye,” though this term remains undefined. This entry however justifies the assumption made in Serial Number 17 that “Byes” had always been a recognised means of scoring.
A fresh bowler is allowed two trial balls, but having taken them, he must then complete the four-ball over.

The “No ball” Law was again modified with the object of curbing round-arm bowling. The resulting Law was so complicated that in fact it materially assisted the sponsors of the “march of intellect” in their campaign. (Vide Chapter 2.)
bold_text: The “No ball” Law was again modified with the object of curbing round-arm bowling.

particulars: The changes listed in Serial Numbers 59 to 61 were almost certainly made in 1819, as G. B. Buckley has traced a Press notice of a match played in Hampshire on June 29th of that year, described as being the first “played out of London with the wicket two inches higher than usual.”
bold_text: The changes listed in Serial Numbers 59 to 61 were almost certainly made in 1819,
annotation: Handwritten: In September of the same year The Leeds' Mercury referred to the changes as ones which seem to be generally adopted.

particulars: The Wicket is increased to measure 26 by 7 inches.
The distance of the Popping crease from the wicket is increased to 4 feet as a result of the increase in the height of the wicket.
The striker is out “Hit wicket” if any part of his dress breaks the wicket.

Substitutes are not to bowl, keep wicket, field at point, middle wicket or long stop (to a fast bowler), except by agreement. A direction that the umpires must be punctilious in enforcing this Law was omitted in 1827, but was restored by 1830.
The selection of the pitch is left entirely to the umpires, i.e. the opponents need no longer select a centre within 30 yards of which the wickets would be pitched by the umpires.
After rain the pitch may be changed by mutual consent.
The Bowling crease is increased to 6 feet 7 inches with Return creases at each end of it at right angles.
The allowance for “Lost ball” is increased from four to six runs.

The “L.B.W.” Law is altered to require the ball to have been delivered in a straight line to the wicket, and to have struck any part of the batsman's person. This alteration was certainly designed to assist the bowler. As the 1788 rule required that the ball should pitch straight, the first clause must have encouraged the round-arm supporters, and its inclusion appears to have been contrary to the M.C.C.'s current policy (vide Chapter 2).

The Wicket is increased to measure 27 by 8 inches, with the stumps of sufficient thickness to prevent the ball from passing through, and with bails 8 inches long. This change is almost certainly that mentioned in Bell's Life of June 27th, 1823, as “newly adopted.” (Vide G. B. Buckley, Fresh Light on Pre-Victorian Cricket.)
bold_text: The Wicket is increased to measure 27 by 8 inches, with the stumps of sufficient thickness to prevent the ball from passing through, and with bails 8 inches long. This change is almost certainly that mentioned in Bell's Life of June 27th, 1823, as “newly adopted.”

particulars: The Bowling crease is increased to 6 feet 8 inches to conform with the width of the wicket.

As a sequel to the experimental round-arm matches played in 1827 already discussed in Chapter 2, the “No ball” Law was adopted in a simplified form leaving it crystal clear that the bowler must keep his hand and arm below the elbow.
The allowance for a “Wide” is to be entered as such and no longer as a “Bye.”
A penalty for a “No ball” is introduced for the case in which no run is otherwise obtained.
An old provision permitting the bowler to water his run up to the wicket is deleted.

The Revision of 1835: every evidence that this was the most thorough revision undertaken up to that time; it must have started in 1834 as the proposed alterations were publicly advertised before the end of that year. The Laws were presented for adoption at the Anniversary Meeting of the M.C.C. held on May 14th, 1835, when there was only time to deal with Serial Number 74, and the remainder of the code was referred to a special Committee which sat on May 19th. A Special Meeting held on the following day confirmed the recommendations of the Committee.

The “No ball” is altered to legalise round-arm bowling in the following terms, “The ball must be bowled. If it be thrown or jerked, or if the hand be above the shoulder in the delivery, the umpire must call ‘No ball’.”
Substitutes, even with consent, may not bowl, keep wicket, field at point, cover point, or long stop—in the last-named position the embargo now applies to every type of bowling.

A Law to prohibit umpires from betting appears later in the day than might be expected, since the selling of matches had become a scandal many years earlier. Either side is given power to dismiss an offending umpire.
The limit of 38 inches for the length of the bat is introduced.
The first “follow on” Law appears obliging a side to bat again if 100 runs behind on the first innings.
A fresh bowler is allowed two trial balls, but if he takes even one, he must then finish the over.
The umpire is again instructed to call “Over” after the four balls have been bowled.
The umpire is specially enjoined to call “No ball” immediately on delivery, and “Wide” as soon as the ball has passed the striker.
annotation: [transcriber] Two ref pairs printed: 71/89 against the first line, 74/90 against the second; by content 71->89 is the Wide chain and 74->90 the No-ball chain, so the printed line order looks crossed. Kept as printed.

particulars: The ball is to be regarded as “dead” on the call of “Wide,” so that no more than the penalty of one run can be reckoned.
For an appeal to be entertained it must be made before the next ball is bowled.
The size of the ball is specified for the first time; it must measure between 9 and 9¼ inches in circumference.

Although often referred to in earlier unofficial editions of the Laws, it is specifically stated for the first time officially that each wicket consists of three stumps, of equal and sufficient thickness to prevent the ball from passing through.
Trial balls are no longer allowed to a fresh bowler.
If one bail remains in place, the removal of the remaining bail renders the wicket “down” for the purpose of a “Run out,” without the necessity of striking a stump from the ground.
Practice with the bat is prohibited during play.
The “L.B.W.” Law reverts to the 1788 version which required a ball to have been pitched straight irrespective of the line of its delivery.
The interval between innings reverts to 10 minutes.

The batting side is allowed to reckon all the runs resulting from a “Wide”—the ball is no longer “dead” on the call of “Wide.” This was a decision of the M.C.C. Committee which seems to have been brought into use at once, though it was not officially confirmed until the Anniversary Meeting of the following year.
bold_text: This was a decision of the M.C.C. Committee which seems to have been brought into use at once, though it was not officially confirmed until the Anniversary Meeting of the following year.

particulars: The umpires are to call “No ball” if not absolutely satisfied that the hand is below the shoulder in delivery.
A “Wide” is defined as a ball not “fairly within the reach of a batsman.” At the same time it is made clear that it is not a “Wide” if the striker moves to bring himself within reach of the ball.
The umpires are required to change ends after each side has had one innings.
Subject to a request by either side being made to the umpires within one minute of the end of an innings, permission is given for the pitch to be swept and rolled between the innings.
The consent of the opposite side is required to the particular player required to act as fielding substitute, and to the place in which he may field.
A runner may be allowed for an injured striker, who however is liable to be run out if either he or his runner is out of their ground while the ball is in play.
The limit of runs for a “follow on” is reduced to 60 runs in the case of a one-day match, and to 80 in the case of a game of longer duration.
A batsman who retires may only resume his innings by consent of the fielding side.

The direction given in Serial Number 90 is reinforced to include not only the instant of delivery, but also the bowler's action immediately beforehand. (For particulars of the instructions issued to the umpires on this subject, vide Chapter 3.)
bold_text: but also the bowler's action immediately beforehand. (For particulars of the instructions issued to the umpires on this subject, vide Chapter 3.)

particulars: The rolling of the pitch between innings to be at the request of the side next to bat.

It was decided to alter the “L.B.W.” Law to render the striker liable should he stop the ball with any part of his person between wicket and wicket, irrespective of the pitch of the ball, or whether it would have hit the wicket or not. This decision was not put into practice as the M.C.C. found that the resolution was out of order owing to notice not having been given in accordance with the rules. (Vide Chapter 3.)
bold_text: It was decided to alter the “L.B.W.” Law to render the striker liable should he stop the ball with any part of his person between wicket and wicket, irrespective of the pitch of the ball, or whether it would have hit the wicket or not.

particulars: A proposal to allow over-arm bowling was not accepted at a General Meeting of the M.C.C. in 1863, but is now approved in the terse phrase, “The ball must be bowled.”
Provided he does not bowl more than two overs in succession, a bowler may change ends twice but no more often in an innings.

The pitch may be rolled for 10 minutes before the start of play. This change is interesting since it emanated from the County Secretaries, a reflection of the increasing prestige of County cricket. Although the change was decided on in 1883, it was not promulgated until the publication of the new code in the following year.
bold_text: This change is interesting since it emanated from the County Secretaries, a reflection of the increasing prestige of County cricket. Although the change was decided on in 1883, it was not promulgated until the publication of the new code in the following year.

particulars: The 1884 Code: the preparation of this Code has been fully described in Chapter 4, from which it will be clear that its introduction involved no major changes in the conduct of the game.

For the first time reference is found to the number of players on each side, to the number of innings, to the method by which runs are scored and the results of matches assessed, to the appointment of umpires and scorers,
and throughout the revision free use is made of the term “Dead ball” about which previously there were no very explicit instructions.
The thickness of the bail is specified for the first time to remove doubts about the overall height of the wicket.
“Boundaries” are officially mentioned for the first time, though they were in use many years earlier.
A last-minute addition was made to the “No ball” Law to make it clear that the umpire must call if not absolutely satisfied of the fairness of a delivery.
Three Laws dealing with one-day cricket were removed from the general code and shown separately.
It is interesting to note that the opportunity was not taken to revive the 1863 proposal to amend the “L.B.W.” Law.
All the changes mentioned above in no way altered the intent of the earlier Laws, and the only important alterations are as follows:
A striker becomes liable to be out for any infringement of the Laws by his runner — previously only his liability in respect of a run out had been mentioned.
The umpires are to be appointed “one for each end”—a truly significant phrase.

Although the term “Bye” is found much earlier in the Laws for Single-wicket, and clearly both Byes and Leg Byes were a recognised means of scoring, they are now specifically defined for the first time.
The Law defining a wicket being “down” confirms that if one bail is off, the fall of the remaining bail suffices without the need to strike a stump from the ground.
The “Obstruction” Law is extended to cover not only the obstruction of a catch but now any form of such tactics by either batsman; except in the former case either batsman is liable to be dismissed.
The Over is increased from four balls to five.
A bowler is permitted to change ends as often as he pleases, but may not bowl two overs in succession in any innings.
The batting side is allowed to declare its innings closed at any time on the last day of a match.
The limit of runs for a “follow on” is increased to 120 runs in a three-day match. The Law still however provides no option in its application.
The ball becomes “dead” if it lodges in the batsman's clothing.
Either umpire may call “No ball” if not satisfied with the absolute fairness of any delivery.
The enforcement of a “Follow on” becomes optional for the side in the lead. The limits are altered to: for a three-day match 150 runs, for a two-day match 100 runs, and for a one-day match 75 runs.
A declaration is allowed in a three-day match after the start of the luncheon interval on the second day.
The Over is increased from five balls to six.
The Bowling Crease is lengthened to 8 feet 8 inches.
In a two-day match a declaration on the first day is allowed provided 100 minutes remain for play.
A declaration is allowed at any time on the second day of a three-day match.
The striker cannot be out stumped off a “No ball,” but may be run out—this change was destined to cause much difficulty in interpretation.
If the start of play is delayed by weather, the “follow on” and “declaration” rules are to apply in accordance with the number of days remaining after the actual start of play.
The ball is to measure between 8 13/16 and 9 inches in circumference.
The limit of runs for a “follow on” in a three- or more day match is altered to 150 runs.
Serial Number 119 is extended to apply in a match of more than three days.
The height of the wicket is increased to be not less than 27 inches nor more than 28 inches—in the latter case the width to be 9 instead of 8 inches.
The time allowed for sweeping and rolling the pitch before the start of each day's play and between the innings is reduced to 7 minutes.
It is made clear that the penalty of 5 runs for irregular fielding is in addition to any runs already made.
The “L.B.W.” Law is extended to include the case of a ball pitching on the off-side of the wicket, provided it hits some part of the striker between wicket and wicket.

The 1947 Code: since the reasons leading up to the revision of the Laws in 1947 have been fully explained in Chapter 5, no special further introduction is now required. Apart from the definite alterations set out later the most important features are as follows:
A definition of the term “Pitch” is included, and the use of the term “Wicket” is confined to the stumps and the bails.
The term “Special Regulation” is defined in order to provide for any special playing conditions agreed upon as necessary to meet the requirements of differing climates, competitive cricket and so on.
A new Law is included to collect and expand all the many references to the ball becoming “dead” previously scattered throughout the 1884 code.
The “L.B.W.” Law is more closely defined in respect of a ball hitting the striker either full-pitch or above the level of the bails.
The umpires are no longer required to pitch the wickets, but are to satisfy themselves that they have been properly pitched.
The batting captain has the right to say where a fielding substitute may not field; previously he was required to say where he should field. N.B. Subject to consent a substitute may keep wicket.
The provision of a new ball at the start of an innings is no longer obligatory in every class of cricket.

A major change is made in respect of the final over of a match. Previously the batting side alone had the option of continuing play if a wicket fell within two minutes of “Time,” but now the last over of any match must be finished if either captain so demands.
Latitude is provided for the “Over” to be of either 6 or 8 balls in order to meet the requirements of cricket overseas.
The new “Dead ball” Law for the first time states when the ball ceases to be “dead.”

The “No ball” Law no longer requires the bowler to have his back foot “grounded” at the instant of delivery, though it must still be behind the line of the Bowling crease. Previously umpires had found it impossible to adjudicate on this point, and as a matter of course had disregarded the old instruction.
It is made clear that the striker cannot create a “Wide” by stepping back.
Whereas before it had been ruled that the least disturbance of a bail sufficed for the wicket to be “down,” it is now necessary for the bail to fall clear of the grooves on the stumps.

The Laws regarding “Running out” and “Stumping” revert to the original eighteenth-century conception, in order to eliminate many difficulties of interpretation which previously existed. It is now ruled that when the wicket-keeper puts down the wicket, the striker is not to be given “Run out” unless in the opinion of the umpire he is attempting a run.

The old Laws were obscure on the point of the wicket-keeper taking the ball in front of the wicket. The Law now states that he must remain behind the wicket until the striker plays the ball, or the ball passes the wicket, or the striker attempts a run.

Previously no mention was made to the incommoding of the striker by any fieldsman except the wicket-keeper. This is now corrected by bringing obstruction of this nature within the judgment of the umpires in respect of unfair play.
